GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Early Wednesday, a deeper pool of moisture lifts into the Four Corners ahead of the previously mentioned system. This is expected to produce more substantial rainfall for southern CO and southeast UT.
GJT.text:
A weak disturbance spinning up into the Southwest this afternoon will send some cloud cover across the region late this evening and Sunday. This will aid the cool trend in temperatures continuing Sunday and Monday. While moisture looks anemic with this wave, it does look like we manage to get some light rain into southeast UT and southwest CO Sunday afternoon and evening. Freezing levels remain high enough to isolate snow to above treeline in the San Juans, where very little snow is expected anyway. Weak shortwave perturbations continue to ripple across the southern half of the CWA on Monday and Tuesday, ahead of a deeper more organized system coming ashore out west. Stronger southwest flow will return temperatures to the normal range Tuesday and Wednesday.

Early Wednesday, a deeper pool of moisture lifts into the Four Corners ahead of the previously mentioned system. This is expected to produce more substantial rainfall for southern CO and southeast UT. This could also produce some additional snowfall for the mountains, depending on depth of cold air on the backside of this system. Cooler temperatures return Friday and Saturday as cold air pools in the region, while unsettled conditions continue for the mountains.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Upper level flow will turn more southerly on Thursday, and this is when the bulk of the Pacific moisture plume will arrive.
BOU.text:
Not a cloud in the sky today across our area with soundings and current observations showing 40-50 degree dewpoint depressions and a dry vertical profile. Winds will remain light, with the exception of the easternmost Colorado plains, where southerly winds at 10-15 mph with sporadic gusts up to 25 mph will be possible. As such, elevated to locally critical fire weather conditions may occur over portions of Lincoln and Washington counties this afternoon although these conditions should be short-lived. High temperatures this afternoon are expected to be in the mid 70s for the low elevations, while the mountains experience a wider range of temperatures in the 50s and 60s. Cloud cover from a decaying disturbance will drift over the region tomorrow leading to temperatures a few degrees cooler than today, though still in the low 70s for the plains and Denver metro.

A return to southwest flow aloft and a weak shortwave will bring a slight chance (15-25% PoPs) for some rain and snow showers over the high terrain Monday, although no snow accumulation is expected and rainfall amounts will reach a trace at most.

An upper level trough will start to deepen off the Pacific Northwest coast late Monday night. This upper level trough will slide south and become a strong cutoff low as it approaches the California coast and begins to move east on Wednesday. Southwest flow aloft will intensify across the Four Corners region ahead of this cutoff low on Wednesday afternoon, bringing increasing moisture and precipitation chances for the high country late Wednesday into Thursday.

Upper level flow will turn more southerly on Thursday, and this is when the bulk of the Pacific moisture plume will arrive. However, as it stand now, our area will likely be under a downsloping regime with south-southwesterly flow favoring orographic lift over southwestern Colorado and the San Juan Mountains primarily. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Can't rule out some spotty shower from Sunday night into mid week. A much better chance of showers will develop by later Wednesday and last into Saturday. \/Hodanish
PUB.text:
For the CONTDVD region, especially the SW mountains...

It still is looking quite wet over the southwest mountains during the long term forecast period. Persistent moist southwest flow is going to evolve through the period. The first round of precip will start Sunday night and last into early Tuesday. This precip ia associated with the first shortwave moving across the SW mtn region. This system is rather warm and there is not too much forcing with it, so only expect light rain showers (with very high elevation snow showers). A much more substantial trough will evolve along the Pacific west coast and eventually move over the SW mtn region by late week. Precip with this 2nd more significant system will enter the SW mtns late Wednesday and likely last into the weekend. Precip with this 2nd system is likely to be substantial, and we are going to have to be concerned with flooding over the San Juans with this system. The San Juan river basin has been running quite high from the previous storm and the grounds across this region are already saturated, so it is not going to take too much precip for potential flooding problems. Of interest, the National 0-7 day WPC QPF chart issued at 10:29 UTC Saturday shows that the greatest amount of precip to fall over CONUS during the next 7 days will fall over the greater San Juan mountains of Colorado (to be fair, some hefty QPF amounts are also expected over the Outer Banks of NC and far south Florida also). 3-4" of liquid precip are expected. As for snow, I don't think we will see impactful snow until the trough (and associated colder air) gets closer towards the weekend time period.

A weak boundary will push through Sunday night and this will cool down the plains few degrees for Monday. Expect mainly max temps in the 65-70 degree range this day with mostly partly sunny skies.

For the rest of the week, warming up with temps mainly in the 70s through the period and it will likely be dry.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The upper level low will make its exit to the east sometime in the Friday through Sunday period. This will present the next chance for notable precipitation, while also dropping temperatures closer to seasonal normals.
CYS.text:
Warm and dry weather is expected to continue through most of next week, though a transition to a more active pattern is possible by the end of the week into next weekend. The synoptic weather pattern for the weak ahead will features a broad ridge over the central US, with another slow moving closed low meandering into the western part of the country. Southwest flow aloft will prevail through most of the week. Temperatures will be well above seasonal averages with 700- mb temperatures around +5 to +8C for much of the week. Look for highs in the mid 60s to mid 70s across the area, which will be about 10-15F above normal. The flow direction will continue to improve mid to upper level moisture through the week. By Thursday afternoon, NAEFS mean precipitable water is actually quite close to climatological maximums. Despite the high moisture content, we don't have much lift to actually translate this into precipitation. Weak heating this late in the season will keep convective instability to a minimum, and synoptic forcing appears unimpressive at this time. Still, we may see some widely scattered high-based showers each afternoon and early evening through the week ahead. Forcing may be strong enough by Thursday to pick up coverage a little as the upper level low to our west inches closer. Fortunately, the moisture advection will mix into the boundary layer periodically, which should keep fire weather concerns down.

The upper level low will make its exit to the east sometime in the Friday through Sunday period. This will present the next chance for notable precipitation, while also dropping temperatures closer to seasonal normals. Most likely, Friday will be another warm day but with increasing chances for rainfall later in the day, with the cool- down waiting until Saturday. Since we are still 6 to 7 days out, precipitation is highly uncertain at this time. NBM PoPs are generally in the 30 to 50% range which seems appropriate at this lead time. SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Tuesday onward will see the deepening northern stream cutoff another broad low across the western CONUS before gradually translating eastward through the Great Basin and Intermountain West.
SLC.text:
Another pleasant weather day underway across the region today. Much like Friday, temperatures are running around 5-10 degrees below seasonal normal across south to southeast Utah, and near normal elsewhere. Water vapor and visible satellite show moisture/cloud cover lifting into southern Utah around a cutoff low, but dry conditions are expected to be maintained throughout the daytime hours Saturday.

The cutoff low and associated moisture will gradually get tugged northeastward into the northern jet. Low end (~10-30%) shower chances then creep into portions of southern Utah overnight into Sunday, with a few isolated thunderstorms also possible Sunday afternoon. While instability is limited, PWAT anomalies to around 200% of normal will support at least some localized threat of a couple cells with more moderate rain rates. While widespread flash flooding is not anticipated, have introduced "Possible" ratings in the Flash Flood Potential to Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, the Grand Staircase, and Zion, and primarily for the more rain sensitive basins in those areas. Similar conditions are anticipated Monday as the low further ejects into the northern stream.

Tuesday onward will see the deepening northern stream cutoff another broad low across the western CONUS before gradually translating eastward through the Great Basin and Intermountain West. Ensemble members still show some differences in how exactly this transpires, with some members now showing some potential for a brief dry slot Wednesday. Broadly speaking though, ample moisture advection into the area in combination with strong synoptic forcing will support increased chances of widespread precipitation Tuesday through Friday (excluding Wednesday if the dry slot develops). Chances likely will be maximized in the Thursday/Friday time frames as ensembles favor that window for when the trough axis passes through the local forecast region. BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The closed low will slow its southern progression off the central/southern CA coast on Tuesday, as a northern trough approaches the BC, Canada coast. Slight cooling aloft and increased cloud cover will take 3 to 5 degrees of high temperatures on Tuesday.
BOI.text: The closed low will slow its southern progression off the central/southern CA coast on Tuesday, as a northern trough approaches the BC, Canada coast. Slight cooling aloft and increased cloud cover will take 3 to 5 degrees of high temperatures on Tuesday. Models are showing marginally favorable convective parameters over the w-central Idaho and eastern Boise Mtns, which are covered by a 20-30% chance of showers for Tuesday afternoon. The closed low turns east, then northeast Wed-Fri as it gets picked up by the northern stream trough tracking along the US/Canada border. Most areas see a chance of precipitation during this period, through the track of the low continues to favor SW Idaho zones with the greatest coverage and amounts. The heaviest rainfall (and mtn top snowfall) totals remain focused over w-central Idaho with widespread 0.25-0.50 inch amounts and locally up to 0.75 inches for Thur/Fri. Snow levels will drop from 9-10kft MSL Wed/Thur to 6-8kft MSL on Friday as the wrap around precipitation ends. Friday and Saturday are the coolest days as the low lifts through northern Utah and into SE Idaho.
